1:
Henry begins by explaining the proportions of the two histories. The destruction Josiah made of the idols was told at length in the older book and is barely mentioned here; the passover, which that book touched on in a sentence, is what this chapter gives in full. Henry then places the feast among the rest: many were the appointed feasts, but the passover was the chief of them. It opened the series on the night Israel came out of Egypt and closed it on the night Christ was betrayed, and it was in celebrating it that Hezekiah and Josiah — the two great reformers — revived religion in their several days. He carries the point forward to the Lord's supper, which resembles the passover more nearly than any other Jewish festival, and observes that its due observance is both a sign and a means of purity in churches and of devotion in individual Christians.

Delitzsch attends to the date and to the shape of what follows. The opening verse is a heading rather than a narrative step, and the killing of the passover on the fourteenth day of the first month puts this feast exactly at the time the law fixed — which, he notes pointedly, is not how it fell out under Hezekiah. He then maps the chapter: the preparations first, with priests and Levites assigned their services; then the providing of the animals; then the sacrifices and the preparing of the meals; and last the assessment of the festival as a whole.

The setting of the priests in their charges is read alike by three witnesses. Gill has them placed in their offices and proper stations to execute them; Ellicott renders the phrase literally as over their wards; Delitzsch explains that the divisions were assigned the service belonging to each, and that the strengthening the text speaks of was done by encouraging speech and by instruction in what the law required of them. Ellicott says the same in fewer words — exhortation and instruction.

The Levites are addressed by a description as much as a title, and the description matters. Gill takes their teaching office concretely: their business was to go through the tribes instructing the people in the knowledge of God, his word and his worship; he adds that one old manuscript reads the phrase quite differently, as those who prepared the holy things for all Israel. Delitzsch treats the written form as a rare substantive meaning the teachers, while suspecting it a copyist's slip for the commoner word the marginal reading supplies. Ellicott glosses the second description, holy to the Lord, as separated to his service.

Then the command about the ark, where the witnesses genuinely part. Ellicott takes it to imply that the ark had been removed from the inner sanctuary and is now to be restored, and suspects the removal happened under one of the idolatrous kings. Clarke reads the same displacement but attributes it to the priests rather than to the desecrators: they had likely secured the ark when they saw those kings destroying everything that might lead people back to the true God, and now that matters were settled it could be returned. Delitzsch reads the sentence as being about the Levites rather than the ark — they are told they need no longer carry it on their shoulders as they had through the wilderness and until the temple was built, because it now has a fixed place. On his reading the verse ends an obligation; on the others it repairs an outrage.
4:
The Levites are told to prepare themselves by their fathers' houses and courses, and Gill reads the instruction practically: they were to be ready for the work, diligent in it, and to perform it according to the law of God. The written directions of David and of Solomon govern the arrangement, so the order being restored is an old one rather than a new invention.

Where they were to stand, and in what relation to the people, occupies the other witnesses. Gill and Wesley both place the standing in the court of the priests, Wesley noting that the verb often carries the sense of ministering rather than merely being present. Ellicott gives the fullest account of the arrangement and it is genuinely illuminating: the Levites were distributed according to the sections of the lay father-houses, with a portion of a Levitical father-house set beside every whole house of laymen. Delitzsch reads the same clause the same way and states its upshot in four words — serve your brethren the laymen.

Ellicott also sets out what that service actually consisted of, which the chapter only discloses piecemeal later: the Levites were to kill the lambs and skin them, hand the blood to the priests, and give the people their share of the roasted flesh. The division of labour runs from the layman's animal through Levitical hands to the priest at the altar and back again.

One detail in the sequence catches Delitzsch's eye. The command runs kill, sanctify yourselves, prepare — with the sanctifying oddly placed between the two actions rather than before both. He offers a practical explanation: the Levites, having slaughtered the animal, had to wash before handing the blood to the priest for sprinkling. The purification is not a preliminary to the whole service but a step inside it, required at the moment they passed from butchery to the altar.

The animals themselves were the king's gift. Gill counts the thirty thousand lambs and kids as enough to serve thirty thousand families, which is how he reads the figure — households provided for rather than individuals. Delitzsch notes only that the king gave small cattle, lambs and young goats, all of them for passover offerings and all for those present.
8:
The king's gift is matched by others, and the question of who gave draws the passage's one flat contradiction. Gill takes the princes here to be ecclesiastical rather than secular, and reads the following names as proving it — men who were rulers of the house of God. Delitzsch takes the same word to mean the princes of the kingdom, the king's own great men, and treats the ecclesiastical rulers named next as a separate matter. The text supports either reading depending on how tightly the names are bound to the title before them, and neither witness acknowledges the other's alternative.

What the gift was for is clearer than who made it. Gill observes that it reached beyond the families the king's bounty had covered, going to poor priests and Levites whom that bounty had not touched. Delitzsch reads the key word as naming a freewill offering rather than describing the manner of giving, and rejects the adverbial construction another scholar had proposed — so the sentence records a category of offering, not merely that the princes gave willingly.

The chiefs of the Levites then gave to their own, and the figures are larger than the priests received: five thousand small cattle and five hundred oxen, against twenty-six hundred and three hundred. Delitzsch lists the names without comment, and the arithmetic makes its own point about which order was the more numerous, since the same reckoning of a beast to a household implies far more Levitical houses than priestly ones to be provided for.

With that the preparation closes. Gill says everything was got ready for the passover and for the feast of unleavened bread together, and for all sorts of people, rich and poor — which is what the successive gifts have been building toward. Ellicott renders the summary simply as the preparations being completed, and the phrase about the priests' place as their standing on their station. Delitzsch marks the same verse as the hinge: what was arranged in the preceding verses is now carried out, with the priests at their posts and the Levites in their courses, exactly as the king had commanded.
11:
The killing is described as a relay, and all three witnesses trace the same hand-to-hand sequence. Gill says simply that the Levites killed the lambs. Delitzsch sets out the whole motion: the Levites slew the victims, the priests sprinkled the blood from the hand that gave it them, and the Levites flayed the carcasses. Ellicott adds the detail that makes the phrase intelligible — the Hebrew has hand in the singular, meaning the hand of the Levites who caught the blood as they slaughtered and passed it on.

Ellicott then makes a historical observation the others do not. Under Hezekiah, Levites flaying the victims had been an exception forced by circumstance; here it is simply how the thing is done. The emergency measure of one reign has become the settled practice of another, which is a quiet index of how far the Levitical order had been rehabilitated in the interval.

What was removed and given away is read two ways by Gill and one by the others. He allows that the burnt offerings might be those animals set aside for that purpose and separated from the paschal victims, or alternatively the portions taken out of each animal to be burnt — the fat of the inwards, the kidneys, the caul upon the liver. Ellicott takes the second sense without hesitation and explains why the parts can be called the burnt offering at all, since no burnt offering proper was appointed for the passover evening: they are simply the pieces that had to go to the altar. Delitzsch keeps to the text's own logic, that these were taken away in order to be given to the divisions of the lay houses, and so offered as the book of Moses directs.

The cooking divides along the same line as the offerings. The paschal flesh was roasted in the fire as the ordinance required; the consecrated things — which Delitzsch and Ellicott both identify as the oxen — were boiled in pots and caldrons and pans. Ellicott stresses the haste with which the Levites carried the cooked meat out to the laity, and notes that the account is not confined to the evening of the fourteenth but runs on into the days that followed. Gill anchors the roasting where the others do, in the ordinance given by Moses.
14:
The order of serving is the point of these verses, and it runs downward from the laity. Gill notes that the Levites made ready for themselves and for the priests only afterwards, meaning both the paschal lambs and such parts of the peace offerings as fell to them. Delitzsch explains the reason the priests had to be waited on rather than providing for themselves: they were occupied until nightfall with the burnt offerings and the fat, and could not break off. He records that most expositors take the term for the fat to mean the fat of the paschal lambs specifically.

The same principle governs the singers and the gatekeepers. Delitzsch reports that the sons of Asaph stood in their place by the commandment of David and of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun the king's seer, and that the porters kept every gate and might not leave their posts — for which reason their brother Levites prepared their portion for them too. Gill places the singers in the court of the priests, singing and playing while the sacrifices were being offered. Nobody who had a station left it; the men without stations fed those who had. Delitzsch treats that as the arrangement's whole logic rather than an incidental kindness — the service could only run continuously if the men tied to it were provisioned by men who were not.

Then the summary. Gill takes it to cover every sacrifice and every sort of person. Ellicott reads the phrase about the same day as meaning at that time, and explains the burnt offerings mentioned in it as the burning of the fat of the passover victims and of the peace offerings — the verse gathering up the foregoing account rather than adding to it.

The duration closes the section. Gill fixes the passover in its proper time, the fourteenth of Nisan, and Delitzsch adds the seven days of unleavened bread that followed, from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of the same month. The exactness is the thing being reported: this feast was kept on the day the law named, which is what the chapter has been building toward since its first verse.
18:
The assessment is superlative, and Gill itemises what earned it: the feast was kept so exactly according to the law, so universally by Israel and Judah together, and with such liberality on the part of the king and of the chief men among the priests and Levites. Three things, and none of them is the scale of the crowd by itself.

Delitzsch notices that the two histories date the comparison differently. This book says there had been no passover like it since the days of Samuel the prophet; the older account reaches further back and says since the days of the judges. He does not treat the difference as an error in either, and he reads the closing clause as deliberate rhetoric — an enumeration running from the king through priests and Levites and all Judah and Israel down to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the sentence itself performs the universality it is claiming.

The year is given, and with it the chapter turns. Delitzsch marks the eighteenth year of the reign as the date of the passover and the hinge on which the narrative moves to Josiah's death, and here he draws out a real difference between the two accounts. The older book introduces the catastrophe with a theological preface: that although Josiah turned to the Lord with all his heart and soul and strength, and walked wholly according to the law, so that no king before or after was like him, yet the Lord did not turn from the fierceness of his wrath against Judah, having resolved to remove Judah out of his sight because of the sins of Manasseh.

Delitzsch's point is that this book does not do that. The connecting of the pious king's tragic end to the wrath his reforms could not avert is made explicitly in the other history and is absent here — where the death that follows is told without being first explained. The reader of this chapter meets the disaster unprepared, which is a different effect from the one the older writer arranged. Whether that omission is the chronicler's design or simply the shape of his source, Delitzsch does not say.
20:
Gill sets the scene by what had just been achieved: the temple purified and cleansed of its filth and idolatry, repaired, its service put on a good footing — after which, he says, great prosperity in church and state might reasonably have been expected. Henry counts the years that followed and notes what the chapter does with them. Thirteen years lay between the great passover and the king's death, and we may hope things went well in them; but the narrative passes them over in silence, and Henry supplies the reason he thinks governs the omission. The people, for all the reform, were not turned from the love of their sins, nor God from the fierceness of his anger. The next thing we hear of Josiah is that he is cut off in the midst of his days and his usefulness, not yet forty years old.

The warning from Egypt is given in full, and Delitzsch works through its wording. Necho's message denies any quarrel with Judah — not against thee do I come this day, but against the house of my war — and Delitzsch corrects a natural misreading of that phrase: it does not mean a warlike house but the house with which the war is, the hereditary enemy. The claim that follows is the one Josiah had to weigh, that God had commanded haste and was with the Egyptian, and that resisting would be resisting him.

What Josiah did next Delitzsch reads as a double disguise, and this is the sharpest observation in the chapter. The verb ordinarily means to change one's clothes or to disfigure oneself; here he takes it into the moral realm, so that the king in disguising his person also disfigured his character. Through his whole reign Josiah had laboured to carry out the will of God; in this one action he set himself against a word that claimed to come from God, and the text's choice of verb registers the contradiction. Gill puts the same refusal plainly — he would not withdraw his forces and go back. Neither witness softens what the chapter then says of the warning, that Josiah did not hearken to the words of Necho from the mouth of God.
23:
The archers found him despite the disguise, and Gill explains how: though his dress concealed the king, his bearing did not conceal the commander, and a man evidently in chief command drew their fire. The disguise failed at the only point where it mattered.

What happened after the wound is where the two accounts diverge, and the witnesses handle the divergence carefully. This book has the servants take him from the war chariot, set him in the second one, bring him to Jerusalem, and there he dies. The older account says they made him ride dead — or dying — from Megiddo. Ellicott sets the two side by side and refuses the easy resolution: even if the word cannot properly be rendered dying, he will not accept the suggestion that this chapter's version is an arbitrary alteration of the older one made for literary effect. The divergence, he argues, points rather to the chronicler having material of his own.

Clarke is interested in the second chariot for its own sake, and offers a flat explanation. It may mean no more than that they moved him out of his own vehicle into another, either for secrecy or because the first had been disabled — perhaps the chariot of the officer attending him. Gill reports the outcome without elaboration: they brought him to Jerusalem and buried him there.

The mourning that followed produced a poem that no longer exists, and both Gill and Clarke say so. Gill notes that the lamentation Jeremiah composed for Josiah is lost, and guards against a common identification — the passage sometimes cited for it concerns Zedekiah, not Josiah. Clarke widens the frame: the Hebrews had poetical compositions for every great occasion, military songs, songs of triumph, marriage odes, funeral elegies, generally made by prophets or inspired men, and this one has simply not survived. He passes on the Targum's account, in which the singing men and women kept these lamentations up to the writer's own day and the mourning became an annual statute in Israel. A king whose great achievement was a feast kept exactly on its day ends by becoming the occasion of another fixed observance, this one of grief.
26:
The closing formula is brief, and Ellicott finds in it a phrase that is not brief at all in its implications. The king's goodness — his pious deeds — is said to have been according to what is written in the law of the Lord, and Ellicott points out that this is said of no other king. The formula that closes other reigns records what a king did; this one measures it against a standard, and the measurement comes out level.

Gill sums the same clause in two words, his piety toward God and his liberality to the people, which is how the chapter has in fact presented him — a reformer who paid for the reform out of his own flocks and herds rather than levying it.

The closing formula draws no textual argument from anyone, which is unusual after a chapter contested at almost every verse: there is nothing in it to correct.

On the source cited, Ellicott notes a small difference of title: this book sends the reader to the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, where the older account names the chronicles of the kings of Judah alone. The wider title matches this writer's habit of treating the two kingdoms as one subject.

Clarke closes with the Targum's expansion of the phrase about first and last deeds, and it reads like a table of contents for a book nobody has. The former things Josiah did in his childhood and the latter in his youth; the judgments he pronounced from his eighth year, when he came to the throne, to his eighteenth, when he had grown and began to repair the sanctuary; and what he brought of his own substance to the work of purging the house of Israel and of Judah from all uncleanness. Clarke's own comment on all this is the plainest sentence in the chapter's apparatus: these general histories are lost, and what we have of the leading facts is what stands in the books we possess. The chapter that began by recording a feast in exhaustive detail ends by pointing past itself to fuller records that no longer exist anywhere.
